report:
**Conclusion:** The claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is not supported by reliable evidence. Apple coatings may be natural waxes (including carnauba) or regulated refined petroleum waxes; they are used in small amounts to limit water loss and handling damage.

The strongest evidence *against* the claim is regulatory toxicology. EFSA’s scientific re-evaluation of carnauba wax (E903), a permitted glazing agent, concluded that available data and the absence of structural alerts raised **no genotoxicity concern**; subchronic and reproductive/developmental studies found no adverse effects attributable to intake. It also noted an evidence limitation: no chronic/carcinogenicity studies were available. Thus, this is not proof of zero risk, but it is not evidence that apple wax causes cancer.  
https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2903/j.efsa.2012.2880

In the U.S., FDA guidance says fruit-and-vegetable coating components must be authorized food additives for the applicable use, GRAS substances, or otherwise lawfully used ingredients.  
https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cpg-sec-562550-safety-and-labeling-waxed-coated-fruits-and-vegetables

Refined petroleum wax is specifically permitted under conditions FDA characterizes as safe, with purity specifications—this should not be conflated with unrefined petroleum products or industrial wax.  
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-172/subpart-I/section-172.886

I found online assertions calling apple wax “carcinogenic,” but no credible human study or authoritative cancer assessment supporting that assertion. Washing apples under running water is reasonable for general hygiene, but cancer avoidance is not an evidence-based reason to peel or avoid properly regulated waxed apples.
